author: By Enjoyiana Nururdin
title: Madison City Council election results are in. Here's where races stand
text: All 20 seats on the Madison City Council were up for election this spring. Half of the seats will be up for election every other year. All 20 seats on the Madison City Council are up for election this spring. Half of the seats will be up for election every other year.  Local Government Reporter Local Government Reporter All 20 seats on the Madison City Council were up for election this spring. Half of the seats will be up for election every other year. Editor's note: This article was updated after all precincts were reporting election results. In Madison's 20 City Council elections April 1, the results are now in. Here's where the races stand, according to the Dane County Clerk's Office: District 1 Voters reelected Ald. John Duncan, who ran unopposed. Duncan was first elected to represent part of the far west side two years ago and brings years of health care and legal experience. District 2 William Ochowicz defeated Matt Egerer for this open downtown seat. Ochowicz received 60% of the vote while 38% cast ballots for Egerer. District 3 Ald. Derek Field ran unopposed and was reelected to represent part of east Madison. Field brings experience and education in policy and public affairs. District 4 Voters reelected longtime Ald. Mike Verveer over challenger Eli Tsarovksy for the downtown seat. Verveer has over three decades of experience on the council. He received about 53% of the vote. Tsarovksy received 46%. District 5 Voters reelected Ald. Regina Vidaver over challenger Ulrike Dieterle, 71% to 28% respectively, for the near west side seat. Vidaver brings years of experience in health management and nonprofit leadership. District 6 Uncontested for an open seat, Davy Mayer was elected to represent part of east Madison. Mayer told the Cap Times he plans to bring elements of project management to the role as alder. District 7 On the west side, voters elected civil engineer Badri Lankella to represent them on the council. Lankella defeated Abdi Siad 54% to 46% for an open seat. District 8 Ald. MGR Govindarajan ran unopposed and was reelected to serve in the seat representing mostly University of Wisconsin-Madison students. Govindarajan brings experience as a recent graduate working in state government. District 9 In the Feb. 18 primary election, challenger Joann Pritchett received over 100 votes above Ald. Nikki Conklin. On Tuesday, 51% of voters favored Pritchett to 48% for Conklin in the west side district. District 10 Voters reelected Ald. Yannette Figueroa Cole over challenger Lisa Veldran. The candidates received 53% and 47% of the vote, respectively. Figueroa Cole was first elected four years ago and is the first Latina woman to be council president in Madison. District 11 Ald. Bill Tishler ran unopposed and was reelected to represent this near west side. Tishler first took office three years ago. District 12 Challenger Julia Matthews defeated Ald. Amani Latimer Burris in this north side district, 53% to 46%. Matthews has been challenging Latimer Burris in District 12 for the last two years. District 13 Voters reelected Ald. Tag Evers over challenger Rob Luther. The candidates received 85% and 15% of the votes, respectively. Evers has represented the Lake Wingra area since 2019. District 14 When Isadore Knox Jr. and Noah Lieberman last faced off in 2023, the election ended in a tie. Knox won the south side seat when his name was pulled out of a bag. On April 1, Knox won reelection 52% to 48%. District 15 East side voters reelected Ald. Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford even though she had announced suspending her campaign in January. Martinez-Rutherford had endorsed her opponent, small business owner Ryan Koglin, to succeed her. About 51% of voters cast ballots for Martinez-Rutherford and 48% for Koglin. Martinez-Rutherford could stay in office or decline another term, leaving the seat vacant for the City Council to fill. District 16 Sean O'Brien, the policy director for Fair Wisconsin, which advocates for LGBTQ+ civil rights, was elected to represent this open east side seat over Kim Richman. O'Brien received about 62% of the vote. Richman received 37%. District 17 Ald. Sabrina Madison was reelected in the east side district over challenger Sean Burke, 73% to 26%. District 18 Carmella Glenn defeated Kevin A. Monroe for the open north side seat currently held by Ald. Charles Myadze. Glenn received 74% of the vote. Monroe received 26%. District 19 By nine votes, west side voters favored Ald. John Guequierre to represent this seat over challenger Nino Amato, who told the Cap Times he plans to request a recount. District 20 Ald. Barbara Harrington-McKinney was reelected to represent part of Madison's west side, defeating challenger Sammy Khilji 79% to 20%. Harrington-McKinney has been the alder since 2015. Enjoyiana Nururdin is a local government reporter for the Cap Times. Enjoyiana writes about community, politics, transportation, housing and safety in the Madison region. author: Cap Times editorial
title: Editorial | Democracy may be imperiled elsewhere, but not in Madison
text: Madison City Council Ald. Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford is running for the 76th Assembly District currently represented by state Rep. Francesca Hong, who has launched a campaign for governor. Issues surrounding local elections here in Madison were quickly sorted out in a way that reflected the will of the voters.  Madison City Council Ald. Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford is running for the 76th Assembly District currently represented by state Rep. Francesca Hong, who has launched a campaign for governor. The April 1 election for 20 seats on the Madison Common Council saw the defeats of several incumbents, the election of several able newcomers, and plenty of close results. Two of the contests remained unsettled in the days immediately following the election, but they were quickly sorted out in a manner that reflected the will of the electorate in one of the highest turnout municipal elections in Madison history. That’s a testament to the respect that Madisonians have for the democratic processes that must always underpin local, state and national government. In the east-side contest to fill the District 15 City Council seat, incumbent Alder Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford suspended her campaign in January. Martinez-Rutherford is an impressive council member with strong ties to the district she represented as the first transgender woman elected to the council. Stepping down to focus on personal issues, including a search for affordable housing on the east side and prioritizing her health, she would later explain: “It was one of the hardest decisions, because when trans people get a seat at the table, when poor people get a seat at the table, it's hard for us to continue beyond a first term. Oftentimes it prevents us from entering races like this.” Martinez-Rutherford’s decision not to seek reelection came after the filing deadline for candidates, so her name remained on the April 1 ballot. To clarify the circumstance, she endorsed her opponent, small business owner Ryan Koglin, and that was supposed to settle the matter. The voters had another idea, however. They reelected Martinez-Rutherford by about 200 votes out of almost 7,500 cast. The result gave Martinez-Rutherford an opportunity to switch course, and to continue to represent the district. And she chose to embrace the will of the people, announcing last week: “I will accept, and I will continue to serve District 15 as long as I’m able. I will do so with courage, clarity and deep care. To everyone who believed in me and the possibility of this moment, thank you.” Martinez-Rutherford immediately provided that representation when she pushed back against the absurd notion that the choice to reelect her was a fluke. “This community has always been at the heart of my service, and I never forgot that my name would be on the ballot and there was a potential for people to vote for me,” she explained. “I didn't expect to win, and to suggest that our district — which is known for being highly informed and a highly engaged electorate — didn't know or wasn't informed feels like a slap in the face to the voters.” She’s right. The voters made an unexpected choice. But that’s one of the reasons why elections matter, and we are glad Martinez-Rutherford will serve another term. The other seat where circumstances were complicated was on the west side, where former Alder Nino Amato suffered a narrow defeat in District 19. With just nine votes separating him from incumbent Alder John Guequierre, Amato sought a recount, which was the right thing to do. Though we have long admired Amato, when he ran again for the council this spring, he did not gain our endorsement. We were concerned about whether he was qualified to run in the 19th District. Amato said as the election approached that he was in the process of moving to the district, but state law requires candidates to be residents of districts in which they compete at least 28 days before the election. While we noted our appreciation for Amato’s long commitment to public service, and our concern with the fact that he apparently got bad advice from the city clerk’s office regarding the residency issue, we backed Guequierre, an affordable housing consultant whom we had also endorsed in 2023. On Election Day, west-side voters split almost evenly between the two contenders, with 3,480 backing Guequierre and 3,471 supporting Amato. The razor-thin result was the closest in this year’s crowded field of council races and qualified Amato for a free recount, which reaffirmed the initial result — as is usually the case when election results are reviewed in this manner. As such, the residency question was laid to rest for this election cycle. All the talk of recounts, vacancies and recommendations for replacements can be complicated. But these processes uphold a standard Madisonians should appreciate. When an election is close, or unexpected, candidates have a responsibility to consider how best to assure that the will of the people is reflected in results, and the governing that extends from those results. We are all painfully aware that there have been times when the recount option has been cynically abused. That certainly was the case in 2020, when Republican Donald Trump tried to overturn Joe Biden's victory in Wisconsin, where the Demorat won by 20,000-plus votes in that year’s presidential race. Trump’s claim that he had won the state came to be known as the “Big Lie,” and the Trump team embarrassed itself by forcing a recount that ultimately saw Biden’s winning margin increase. Trump’s disregard for democracy in general, and for Wisconsin democracy in particular, was unsettling. His effort to overturn the results of a legitimately conducted election undoubtedly caused many Wisconsinites to associate recounts and after-the-fact reviews of election returns with sour grapes and abuses of the electoral process. But, for the most part, issues that evolve from close elections with unexpected or complicated results can be sorted out in ways that sustain confidence in democracy. That, to our view, is what happened this spring in Madison, and it is especially worthy of note in these agitated times. author: Arman Rahman
title: 7 new alders sworn in to Madison Common Council after spring election
text: Madison Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes Resize:  Reporter On Tuesday, the Madison City Council changed the guard, turning over seven seats to new faces after the spring election. MADISON, Wis. -- On Tuesday, the Madison City Council changed the guard, turning over seven seats to new faces after the spring election. This includes District 18, bringing the contentious previous term of Charles Myadze to an end, as his trial continues over charges he allegedly beat, strangled, and threatened to kill former Deputy Mayor Gloria Reyes while the two were in a relationship. On Tuesday, Carmella Glenn was sworn in after winning Myadze’s seat. “It’s an exciting day and I'm excited to get started.” She said she’s looking ahead to the future of District 18, and so are the residents who live there. “When you listen to the constituents...what happens inside of systems, they're not real interested,” Glenn said. “And so talking to them, there were a lot of great things that got done by the former alder as far as projects. And so hopefully to step into those and make sure they come to fruition.” She said she wants to focus on food and park access for that part of the North Side, working closely with District 12. “I'd love to see things like Troy Drive be replicated,” Glenn said. “Also, we have some really cool parks, everyone thinks of the North Side (and) they think of Warner. But we have a lot of smaller parks that I love to see access to.” Glenn said she heard from constituents that representation was a concern when Myadze was removed from his committees and censured. “If you want to be part of the decision-making, you got to get to the table where the decisions are made,” she said. “And so I hope to be able to represent all of my district, but I really want Black and brown people to know that our voice matters and we got to show up.” Myadze did not show up in person or virtually to what would have been his final council meeting. His most recent court date was March 27, where a judge declined his attorney's request for a change of venue. While his fellow outgoing alders had their full commending resolutions and contributions read, his was a swift affirmative vote. Amani Latimer-Burris was beaten for her District 12 seat by Julia Matthews. “You got to be independent, you got to ignore the noise, you got to think for yourself, you got to ask a lot of questions even if it annoys people,” Latimer-Burris said at the meeting. Earlier in the day, Latimer-Burris released a city blog post claiming she was one of the people who reported allegations against Myadze last March and April, though she said she told no one she did so. She also said she abstained and recused herself from the censure vote in December because of due process, and because she claimed others on council knew Myadze would be arrested two days later -- claims News 3 Now have not independently verified. After the swearing-in ceremony on Monday, all of Latimer-Burris’s blog posts were deleted, as her alder page was replaced with that of Matthews’. Latimer-Burris did not address the allegations as part of her farewell speech. “This job will make you grow and will make you research yourself, it'll make you look into your soul, because you will come up on an issue where it's going to challenge you and you've got to make the right decision," she said. After not running for re-election in the spring, it was Juliana Bennett’s final meeting as District 2 alder. “We ran to make a change, and the legacy we have doesn't live in ceremonies like this it lives in infrastructure and policy and impact,” she said in a speech. Bennett was first elected at 21 years old back in 2021. She publicly identified herself as one of Myadze’s alleged victims, saying she was only 22 when Myadze allegedly made inappropriate comments to her about her body and clothing, and locked her in his car and yelled at her when she told others, denying anything inappropriate. She did not address any of those allegations or the city investigation Tuesday. RELATED: Complainant speaks out after report finds insufficient evidence that Madison alder violated harassment policy “If we do our jobs well, people's lives will be easier and they won't even know it was us,” Bennett said. Alder Nasra Wehelie bid farewell to the seat she's held since 2020, when she was the first Muslim woman elected to council. District 5 Alder Regina Vidaver, whose map includes the Greenbush, Vilas, and Westmoreland neighborhoods, was voted council president. District 8 Alder MGR Govindarajan was elected vice president. He serves all of the University of Wisconsin-Madison campus, and south-campus neighborhoods east of Randall Ave, north of Regent St, and west of Park St. Below is a list, by district, of all the new alders: District 2 - Will Ochowicz beat Matt Egerer for Juliana Bennett’s seat. District 6 - Davy Mayer ran unopposed for Marsha Rummel’s seat, who also chose not to run for re-election. District 7 - Badri Lankella beat Abdi Siad for Nasra Wehelie’s seat. District 9 - Joan Pritchett beat Nikki Conklin. District 12 - Julia Matthews beat Amani Latimer-Burris. District 15 - Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford won, after dropping out of the race, then accepted the seat. District 16 - Sean O’Brien beat Kim Richman after Jael Currie chose not to run for re-election. District 18 - Carmella Glenn won Charles Myadze’s seat. ​COPYRIGHT 2025 BY CHANNEL 3000.
